metadata.title: Mind the gap: Examining migrant-native disparities in reading performance and subjective wellbeing among 15-year-old students in different education systems
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for a subset of 15 countries, focusing on 15-year-old students’ reading literacy and two subjective wellbeing indicators (happiness and life satisfaction). The manuscript reports that reading scores were computed as the average of 10 plausible values, but it does not describe the application of PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the regression analyses. Because the analysis is implemented as standard multilinear regression (not ML with explicit survey-weight handling), the paper does not provide a weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or any statement about complex survey design adjustments. Analysts using the PISA international database should apply the appropriate student/sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors for population-representative inference; however, this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented, so the degree of design-corrected inference cannot be verified from the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable for reading is derived from PISA plausible values, but the manuscript does not report a missing-data strategy for the regression models (e.g., whether cases with missing covariates were excluded or imputed). This is a reporting gap because PISA background variables (e.g., ESCS, fear of failure, language use at home) can have nontrivial missingness, and the paper reports different N values across models, implying listwise deletion or other handling without explicitly stating it. Without the missing-data protocol, the comparability of coefficients across models and the potential bias from nonresponse cannot be fully assessed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data for an analytic sample restricted to 15 countries grouped into four education-system clusters (early tracking; common core–uniform integration; common core–flexible integration; individualised system). The paper reports that the subset of 15 countries totals approximately 118,000 students for the analytic sample. For gender, responses with invalid/skip/not applicable/no response were excluded; for other variables, the manuscript does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond the model-specific N values.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (15-year-olds) — reading literacy (10 PV average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilinear regression (Table 2): Migration status coefficient = -12.820 (Model 2), p<0.001; Model 2 R-squared = 0.280; N=94716. Education-system models (Table 3): migration coefficient ranges from -19.208 (common core–flexible, Model 2) to -51.448 (individualised system, Model 2); Model 2 R-squared ranges 0.215–0.344.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for 15-year-olds, the study leveraged migration status, grade repetition, language use at home, ESCS, and gender to predict reading performance (mean of 10 plausible values), finding that migration background is associated with a 12.82-point lower reading score after controls and that the migrant-native reading disadvantage is largest in the individualised system (e.g., -51.448 in Model 2). This indicates that integration policies should prioritize language and learning-support interventions for migrant students, with system-specific emphasis where diversity management relies more on individualized support.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilinear regression (Table 2): Migration status coefficient = 0.012 (Model 2), p<0.05; Model 2 R-squared = 0.234; N=94716. Education-system models (Table 4): migration status is statistically insignificant in early tracking (0.015) and individualised system (0.020) but positive in common core–flexible integration (0.044, p<0.001) and common core–uniform integration (0.013, p<0.05); Model 2 R-squared ranges 0.218–0.285.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Subjective wellbeing data for 15-year-olds, the study leveraged migration status, life satisfaction, gender, fear of failure, and education-system cluster to predict happiness, finding that migration is only weakly and inconsistently associated with happiness after controls (positive in some common-core systems but not significant in early tracking and the individualised system). This indicates that wellbeing interventions for migrant students may need to be targeted by education-system context rather than assuming a uniform migrant-native happiness gap.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Subjective wellbeing (15-year-olds) — life satisfaction (rescaled to 1–4)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilinear regression (Table 2): Migration status coefficient = -0.077 (Model 2), p<0.001; Model 2 R-squared = 0.276; N=94716. Education-system models (Table 5): migration status is negative and significant in common core–flexible integration (-0.075, p<0.001) and common core–uniform integration (-0.112, p<0.001) but not significant in early tracking (-0.010) and individualised system (0.058); Model 2 R-squared ranges 0.250–0.338.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Subjective wellbeing data for 15-year-olds, the study leveraged migration status, happiness, gender, fear of failure, and ESCS to predict life satisfaction (rescaled to a 1–4 scale), finding that migration background is associated with lower life satisfaction overall (-0.077 in Model 2) but that the migrant-native life-satisfaction gap disappears in early tracking and the individualised system after controls. This indicates that system-level diversity management and support structures may buffer migrant disadvantages in cognitive wellbeing, so policy should focus on sustaining those protective mechanisms while addressing reading gaps.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds from a subset of 15 countries, examining migrant-native disparities in reading performance and subjective wellbeing (happiness and life satisfaction). Reading is modeled using the mean of 10 plausible values, and the paper estimates multilinear regression models for the full sample and for four education-system clusters (early tracking; common core–uniform; common core–flexible; individualised). Across the full sample, migration background is associated with a 12.82-point lower reading score and a -0.077 lower life satisfaction score after controls, while its association with happiness is small and only weakly significant. Model fit is reported via R-squared (e.g., 0.280 for reading in Model 2). The analysis does not document survey-weight or missing-data handling, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, so results should be treated as associations rather than causal effects.
